strengths: The motivation of the paper is clear and builds on a well studied problem of understanding the role of cross-attention and what they learn in editing T2I models.
The experiments are visually appealing and tell the story of the paper well, especially the weakening of HRVs that shows weakening based on the most and least relevant concepts / heads.
The authors show that using HRVs to edit images works better than SDEdit, P2P, etc.
They also show improvement over Attend and Excite for the problem of catastrophic forgetting in T2I models.
Good motivation and a clear idea.
Comprehensive quantitative and qualitative comparisons with many other solutions.
The experiments, settings, and other details are mainly clearly explained.
This paper provides a new perspective in understanding the features in text-to-image generation: different heads.
Qualitative examples (Figure 3a) and CLIP similarities (Figure3b) along weakening MoRHF and LeRHF clearly show the effect of weakening different heads.
The appendix provides extensive qualitative results to remove doubt for cherry-picked results.
The proposed method is useful for three applications: 1) correcting mis-interpretation of words in t2i generation, 2) boosting prompt-to-prompt, 3) reducing neglect in multi-object generation.
Discussions resolve natural questions: extension to SDXL and effect across different timesteps.
The idea of correlating visual concepts with diffusion models is interesting.
weaknesses: The work does not have new insight compared to previous works such as P2P and Diffusion Self-Guidance regarding the role of cross-attentions.
The idea of manipulating cross-attention maps to control image generation is well-established, and this work primarily extends that by focusing on individual attention heads.
While the authors demonstrate that different heads respond to different concepts, the core mechanism of using attention maps for editing remains similar to prior work.
The disentanglement of heads based on concepts feels like a logical progression rather than a fundamentally new insight into the workings of T2I models.
T2I models could benefit from more comprehensive evaluation on a larger set of generated images / human evaluation.

It requires fixing a set of concepts beforehand for every HRV construction. Does not have a study of how the HRV matrix will be changed when some concepts are changed or replaced after the construction. The method's reliance on a fixed concept set limits its adaptability to dynamic scenarios where concepts might need to be added, removed, or modified. A more robust approach would ideally allow for incremental updates to the HRV matrix without requiring a complete reconstruction.

Manual settings, choice, and configuration are required for every concept (case) during inference (Sec 5.1, Fig 5). The need for manual intervention for each concept during inference introduces a significant practical limitation. This lack of automation hinders the scalability and usability of the method, especially when dealing with a large number of concepts or when real-time adjustments are needed. The process should be streamlined to reduce user burden and improve efficiency.

Lack of failed cases, there are no details about the limitations of this method. The absence of a thorough analysis of failure cases makes it difficult to assess the robustness and reliability of the method. A comprehensive evaluation should include examples where the method fails, along with an explanation of why these failures occur. This would provide a more balanced view of the method's capabilities and limitations.

Even though there is a section for bigger / novel models (SDXL), all experiments, studies, and comparisons are based on SD v1. New models might eliminate many issues the proposed method tries to solve. The exclusive reliance on SD v1 for experiments and comparisons raises concerns about the generalizability of the findings to more advanced models like SDXL. Given the significant improvements in SDXL, it is crucial to evaluate the proposed method on these newer models to determine its relevance and effectiveness in the current landscape of image synthesis.

The paper should provide principles of the proposed approaches; it lacks theoretical justification or intuition for why counting each visual concept with the largest value updates the HRVs, and should include such justification to strengthen the paper.

HRV should be described more clearly; the current description lacks details such as the concatenation axis, notation for K1,…,KN, and proper equations, making it difficult for readers to understand the operation.
Human evaluation should be explained in more detail; Appendix C.2 is insufficient and a table with participant numbers, question types, and quality control measures would strengthen the user study.

The authors should add a textual description of the proposed HRV instead of relying solely on Fig. 2 and Fig. 4; a more detailed explanation of how cross‑attention maps are processed and aggregated, including normalization and combination across layers and heads, would improve clarity.

It is unclear why <SOT> and many <EOT> tokens are required during HRV update; the role of these tokens in the CLIP text encoder and whether they serve as padding or have semantic meaning needs further explanation.

Using SDXL or more recent models such as SD3 as the primary model would be better; reliance on SD1.5 limits applicability to newer diffusion models and raises questions about generalizability to contemporary architectures.

A random weakening baseline should be added in Fig. 3; without it, it is difficult to assess whether the observed performance gains are due to the ordered weakening method rather than any arbitrary weakening of attention heads.
The method should be compared with classifier guidance; the lack of such a comparison makes it hard to assess the relative advantages and disadvantages of the proposed approach.
